subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Religious & Ethical Teachings about Peace & Conflict
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In Just War theory, the conditions that must be satisfied before a war can begin are collectively known as what?
options: Jus ad bellum
Jus in bello
Jus post bellum
Casus belli
questions.explain: Jus ad bellum refers to the conditions justifying going to war, while jus in bello governs conduct during it.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the conditions of a Just War?
options: War must be a last resort after all peaceful means have failed
War may be started for economic gain
War should target civilians to end conflict quickly
War can be declared by any individual citizen
questions.explain: 'Last resort' is a core Just War condition, requiring that all peaceful options be exhausted first.

questions.q: Which two Christian thinkers are most closely associated with developing the theory of the Just War?
options: Augustine and Thomas Aquinas
Martin Luther and John Calvin
Peter and Paul
Francis of Assisi and Ignatius Loyola
questions.explain: St Augustine laid the early foundations and Thomas Aquinas later developed the classic conditions of the Just War.

questions.q: In Just War theory, 'proportionality' means that:
options: the good achieved by the war must outweigh the harm and suffering it causes
as many soldiers as possible should be recruited
the war must be won as quickly as possible
both sides must have equally sized armies
questions.explain: Proportionality requires that the benefits gained are not outweighed by the destruction and suffering caused.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'holy war'?
options: A war fought for a religious cause or in the name of God
A war fought only in self-defence
A war fought without any weapons
A war fought purely to gain territory and wealth
questions.explain: A holy war is fought to defend or promote a religion, such as the medieval Crusades.

questions.q: In Islam, the 'greater jihad' refers to:
options: the inner, personal struggle to live as a good Muslim
a military war against non-believers
the annual pilgrimage to Mecca
the giving of money to the poor
questions.explain: The greater jihad is the individual's inner spiritual struggle to follow Allah and resist temptation.

questions.q: The 'lesser jihad' is best understood as:
options: the outward struggle to defend Islam, which may include armed conflict
the private prayer performed five times a day
the inner struggle against personal temptation
fasting during the month of Ramadan
questions.explain: The lesser jihad is the outward struggle to defend the faith and can, under strict conditions, involve military action.

questions.q: Which Christian group is especially well known for its commitment to pacifism?
options: The Quakers (Religious Society of Friends)
The Jesuits
The Crusaders
The Knights Templar
questions.explain: Quakers reject all violence and war, believing there is 'that of God' in everyone.

questions.q: Which statement best describes pacifism?
options: The belief that war and violence are wrong and disputes should be settled peacefully
The belief that war is always justified to defend a nation
The belief that only holy wars are acceptable
The belief that violence is acceptable whenever it brings victory
questions.explain: Pacifism opposes war and violence, favouring peaceful resolution of conflict.

questions.q: Jesus' teaching to 'turn the other cheek' encourages believers to:
options: respond to aggression without retaliation or violence
always fight back to defend their honour
ignore all suffering in the world
support their country in every war
questions.explain: From the Sermon on the Mount, it teaches non-retaliation and responding to hostility peacefully.

questions.q: The Beatitude 'Blessed are the peacemakers' suggests that Christians should:
options: actively work to bring about peace and reconciliation
avoid all contact with non-believers
only seek peace within their own family
wage wars in order to establish peace
questions.explain: This Beatitude praises those who work to create peace and mend relationships between people.

questions.q: A 'conscientious objector' is someone who:
options: refuses to fight in a war because of their moral or religious beliefs
volunteers eagerly to join the army
leads a country into a holy war
objects only to paying taxes
questions.explain: A conscientious objector declines military service on grounds of conscience, morality or religion.

questions.q: Jesus' command to 'love your enemies' teaches Christians to:
options: show compassion and forgiveness even to those who harm them
seek revenge against those who wrong them
only love fellow Christians
avoid their enemies completely
questions.explain: This teaching calls Christians to extend love and forgiveness beyond friends to enemies.

questions.q: What is meant by 'reconciliation'?
options: The restoring of friendly relationships after a conflict or disagreement
The declaration of war on an enemy
The refusal to ever forgive an enemy
The winning of a war through force
questions.explain: Reconciliation is the bringing together of those in conflict to restore a harmonious relationship.

questions.q: A country is attacked without warning and, after attempting negotiation, defends itself using only enough force to repel the invaders while avoiding harm to civilians. This best reflects the principles of:
options: the Just War theory
a holy war
pacifism
conscientious objection
questions.explain: Self-defence, last resort, proportionality and protecting civilians are all Just War principles.

questions.q: David is a Christian who refuses to join the army because he believes all violence is wrong, quoting 'turn the other cheek'. David is best described as a:
options: pacifist
crusader
Just War supporter
aggressor
questions.explain: Rejecting all violence on religious grounds makes David a pacifist.

questions.q: Which of the Ten Commandments is often used by Christians who oppose war?
options: 'You shall not murder'
'Honour your father and mother'
'Remember the Sabbath day'
'You shall not steal'
questions.explain: This commandment is frequently cited to argue that taking human life in war is wrong.

questions.q: Why do some Christians accept that war can sometimes be justified, despite teachings on peace?
options: They believe war may be a last resort to protect the innocent and restore justice
They believe war should always be the first choice
They believe Jesus encouraged all forms of violence
They believe that peace is unimportant
questions.explain: Just War thinking allows war as a last resort to defend the innocent and uphold justice.

questions.q: After a long dispute, two neighbours meet, forgive each other and rebuild their friendship. This is an example of:
options: reconciliation
retaliation
a holy war
conscription
questions.explain: Restoring a broken relationship through forgiveness is reconciliation in action.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr campaigned for civil rights while insisting his followers never use violence. His approach is best described as:
options: non-violent protest
holy war
just war
armed rebellion
questions.explain: King, inspired by Christian teaching, championed peaceful, non-violent resistance to injustice.
